idiom_name: duck typing plus typing.Protocol for the letter contract (__getattr__ for wholesale forwarding)
implementation_notes: Python needs no envelope for dispatch: any object with the right attributes is a valid letter (duck typing), and typing.Protocol states that contract structurally for type checkers, so a class conforms without inheriting from anything; abc.ABC/ABCMeta is the nominal alternative when the contract should be enforced at instantiation time. A facade class still earns its place when the implementation must be hidden from users of a published API, when construction must be deferred or cached, or when several operations should share one entry point - then the forwarding is written explicitly, or generated wholesale with __getattr__ when the envelope is meant to be transparent. What replaces the classic structure is dynamic dispatch on attributes plus optional structural typing.
code_sketch:
from typing import Protocol

class Letter(Protocol):                     # structural contract, no inheritance needed
    def draw(self) -> str: ...

class Envelope:                             # the facade
    def __init__(self, letter: Letter) -> None:
        self._letter = letter
    def draw(self) -> str:
        return self._letter.draw()          # forwarding
pitfalls: Protocols are checked statically only: isinstance needs @runtime_checkable and then verifies member presence, not signatures, so a wrong letter still fails at call time.

__getattr__-based forwarding misses implicit special-method lookups, which bypass the instance - a forwarded __len__ or __iter__ is invisible to len() and iter() - and it must re-raise AttributeError instead of swallowing it, or every typo silently changes behaviour.
Assignment never copies, so a shared mutable letter is the default outcome; make letters immutable or copy explicitly when the envelope claims value semantics.
